title: Intel Has a Massive Warning for AMD Stock Investors. Is It Time to Book Profits Before Nov. 3?
detail:
Intel Has a Massive Warning for AMD Stock Investors. Is It Time to Book Profits Before Nov. 3?
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 10:42 AM CDT 5 min read
INTC
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) released its third-quarter results on Oct. 29, and shares of the company crashed more than 28% the following day.

The primary reason behind the bloodbath in Intel stock was its weaker-than-expected guidance. Though Intel guided for a strong year-over-year increase in both revenue and earnings, Wall Street was expecting more. However, the sharp drop in personal computer (PC) sales this year offset the impressive gains that Intel enjoyed in the data center segment.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That doesn't bode well for Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD). Let's look at the reasons why.

Image source: Getty Images.

AMD's reliance on the PC market could dent investor confidence in the stock

When AMD released its second-quarter results in August, the company reported a healthy 23% year-over-year increase in revenue from sales of client central processing units (CPUs) for PCs. The segment's revenue landed at $3.1 billion, accounting for 27% of its top line.

Similarly, Intel's revenue from its client computing segment was up by 13% year over year in Q2 to $8.9 billion. However, the script flipped in Q3, with Intel reporting a 5% year-over-year drop in client computing revenue to $8.1 billion. The company blamed poor PC sales for this decline, which isn't surprising as the market has been going through a rough patch due to high memory costs and component shortages.

Counterpoint Research estimates that global PC shipments dropped 21% year over year in Q3. The firm expects Q4 to be even worse, with a 27% drop from the year-ago period. Similarly, Intel noted that the PC decline has accelerated recently amid high costs that are pressuring companies' IT budgets. So, AMD could feel the heat when it releases Q3 results after the market closes on Nov. 3.

Intel also pointed out that PC shipments will drop around 10% in 2027, with "year-over-year declines to be more pronounced during the first half." The situation could improve in the second half of 2027 due to easier comparisons from the year-ago period. However, AMD's client CPU business may face near-term challenges.

Should investors book profits in AMD ahead of its quarterly report?

AMD stock has jumped 90% over the past year, which is why investors may be wondering whether they should take profits off the table. Well, the broader market sentiment on artificial intelligence (AI) stocks suggests that booking profits could be the right move. However, if AMD suffers a steep fall following its Nov. 3 report, it may be a smart idea to buy it for multiple reasons.

title: What to Expect From AMD’s Q3 Earnings
detail:
What to Expect From AMD’s Q3 Earnings
Sneha Nahata
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:00 AM CDT 4 min read
AMD
Trade AMD on Coinbase

A close-up of an AMD office by gehapromo via Adobe Stock

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) will announce its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3. Strong demand for the company's server processors and Instinct artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators from hyperscale data centers and enterprise clients, along with an expanding addressable market, positions AMD well to deliver robust revenue and earnings growth in the quarter.

As demand for AI infrastructure and data-center computing continues to rise — and as AMD's earnings growth accelerates — AMD stock is likely to sustain its growth trajectory even as it trades at a relatively high valuation.

AMD Could Crush Expectations in Q3

AMD appears well-positioned to deliver another strong quarter, supported by accelerating demand across its server CPUs, Instinct AI accelerators, and embedded products.

In Q2 2026, AMD's top line rose 50% year-over-year (YOY) to $11.5 billion, reflecting broad-based demand across its product portfolio. The company's data-center segment was the key growth engine, increasing its share of total revenue to 58% from 42% in the same period last year.

Data-center revenue climbed 107% YOY to $6.7 billion, driven by robust demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct accelerators. The server CPU business is growing at a solid pace and is likely to sustain momentum in the coming quarters.

The data-center AI business is an important driver for AMD's growth outlook. Revenue from this business more than doubled YOY in Q2, supported by increased demand for Instinct accelerators. Adoption of the MI355X continued to broaden as major AI companies expanded deployments across training and inference workloads.

The expansion of AI workloads creates a substantial opportunity for AMD. As enterprises and cloud providers invest in AI infrastructure, demand is likely to extend beyond specialized training systems to inference applications that support the deployment of AI models at scale. A broader range of workloads could therefore expand AMD's addressable market.

Management has indicated that, amid strong customer demand and improving supply conditions, server CPU revenue is expected to increase by more than 80% YOY in the second half of 2026. For full-year fiscal 2027, server CPU revenue is projected to grow by more than 70% YOY from a significantly higher base. The company also expects data-center segment revenue to more than double YOY in 2027.

For Q3 2026, AMD expects revenue to increase by 41% YOY to $13 billion at the midpoint. Management expects strong double-digit growth in the data-center segment to be the primary contributor, with the embedded business also expected to deliver strong growth.

The earnings outlook also appears favorable, supported by revenue expansion and improved product mix. Analysts expect earnings of $1.68 per share, reflecting a 73% YOY increase from $0.97 per share in the prior-year period.

Overall, AMD's upcoming Q3 report should reflect benefits from several favorable growth drivers, including expanding adoption of Instinct accelerators, strong demand for EPYC processors, and improving supply conditions.

Strong Earnings Justify the Elevated Valuation

The rally in AMD stock this year has driven its valuation higher. However, AMD's premium multiple is warranted, as it is likely to deliver solid earnings growth. AMD stock currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 89 times. Although this multiple is significantly higher than Nvidia's (NVDA) forward P/E ratio, it still appears justified given AMD's EPS growth forecast.

Analysts project EPS to grow by more than 117% in fiscal 2027. Beyond the near-term outlook, AMD stands to benefit from increasing investment in AI infrastructure, high-performance computing (HPC), and advanced data-center processors. These structural growth drivers could help the company outperform its previous growth outlook.

At its Financial Analyst Day last year, AMD outlined expectations for revenue to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) exceeding 35% over the next three to five years, along with a target of $20 in annual EPS. Stronger-than-anticipated adoption of its AI and computing products positions the company to surpass its projections and supports the stock's premium valuation.

Is AMD Stock a Buy?

The Q3 report will likely reflect strong growth momentum, supported by rising demand and expanding AI infrastructure spending. AMD's revenue and earnings outlook suggests solid potential upside, while long-term growth targets support its investment case.

A strong earnings release and upbeat forward guidance could continue to support the rally. Overall, analysts maintain a consensus "Strong Buy" rating on Wall Street, reflecting optimism around AMD"s growth prospects.

Key Takeaways

AMD shares fell 10.9% Friday to $505 after Intel's weak PC outlook triggered a chip rout, leaving the stock 23% below its 52-week high.

Lisa Su expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, and AMD's partnership with Meta covers 6 gigawatts of GPUs.

AMD trades at 45.1x forward earnings, and the MI450 ramp could dilute gross margin as memory content rises.

Tuesday's report needs to beat the $13.09 billion revenue consensus and guide the fourth quarter toward a steeper data center ramp.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) had a strong six months. Friday took a big bite out of it.

The stock fell 10.9% to $505 after Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) warned of weak PC demand, putting Intel on course for its worst day ever and dragging chip stocks down with it. AMD is still up 42.4% over six months, but it now sits 23% below its 52-week high of $659.

The timing stings. AMD reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 3, and its biggest AI customer story keeps growing. On October 27, AMD and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) advanced a partnership that already covers 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs.

So did Intel's warning say much about AMD? A little, and less than the selloff suggests.

Why Intel's news hit AMD

AMD still has real PC exposure. Its client business brought in $3.1 billion in the second quarter, up 23%, or about 27% of revenue by my math.

The mix, however, has shifted hard toward servers:

Data center revenue rose 107% to $6.7 billion.

Data center made up 58% of revenue, up from 42% a year earlier.

Gaming fell 31% on lower semi-custom sales.

Total revenue rose 50% to a record $11.5 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $1.66 beat the $1.62 estimate.

Friday's drop wiped out weeks of gains in one session…

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): share price, $ per share, last 6 months (TIKR)

With a five-year beta of 2.45, AMD tends to swing harder than the chip group in both directions.

Helios must carry the next leg

Lisa Su said in the second-quarter release that AI is driving "a significant expansion in demand for compute across all of our markets." The guidance backs her up.

AMD guided third-quarter revenue to about $13 billion, plus or minus $300 million, implying 41% growth. Consensus sits at $13.09 billion of revenue and $1.95 of EPS, with data center revenue expected near $8.27 billion.

Production shipments of the MI450 and Helios rack platform began in September, with a bigger ramp due in the fourth quarter and the first half of 2027. Su now expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, with server CPU revenue up more than 70%.

Key Stats for AMD Stock

Current Price: $504.80

Target Price (Mid): ~$2,340

Street Target: ~$640

Potential Total Return: ~363%

Annualized IRR: ~44% / year

What Happened?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) fell 10.88% to $504.80 on October 30, days before its own November 3 report. The trigger was Intel (INTC:NASDAQ), which guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion and closed down 28.58%. Yet the same report showed Intel's data center revenue up 78%, and data centers made up 58% of AMD's second-quarter revenue.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 7% and Nvidia 4.22%, with Amazon's AI spending plans adding to the worries. AMD fell harder than both as investors reassessed its exposure to the same PC weakness.

Intel Sold Fewer PCs and Pricier Servers

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel CFO David Zinsner said. Intel's client and physical AI group fell 5% to $8.1 billion, and Intel expects client revenue to drop more than 20% from the third quarter.

The data center side moved the other way. Data center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 billion, and Intel's 10-Q credits the server gain to average selling prices up 54%. Intel expects the division to grow by a mid-teens percentage sequentially in the fourth quarter, though a shortage of packaging substrates is limiting how fast it can ramp server output.

AMD's Revenue Sits on the Growing Side

AMD's data center revenue more than doubled to $6.7 billion in the second quarter, while client revenue rose 23% to $3.1 billion, about 27% of sales. Intel is also AMD's main server rival, so its 78% speaks to the strength of demand, not to who is gaining share. The PC slump still costs AMD something. It guided third-quarter client revenue to only slight sequential growth, and a memory-driven PC slowdown into 2027 would weigh on roughly a quarter of its revenue.

AMD Data Center & Client Operating Revenue (TIKR)

Margins Show Where the Mix Is Heading

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 11, Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager of Compute Enterprise AI, was asked about CPU content in gigawatt-scale AI builds. He said the answer depends on the workload, then added, "today, we're saying 1:1 sort of ratio, and it's going to continue to grow." At the same event, Matt Ramsay, AMD's corporate vice president of financial strategy and investor relations, pointed to "driving gross margin dollars very significantly faster than expenses" next year. TIKR consensus has non-GAAP EBIT margin rising from 22.4% in 2025 to around 28% in 2026 and around 34% in 2027.

title: Prediction: 2 Under $1 Trillion Stocks That Will Be Worth More Than Micron 5 Years From Now
detail:
Prediction: 2 Under $1 Trillion Stocks That Will Be Worth More Than Micron 5 Years From Now
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool

Micron (NASDAQ: MU) is one of the most popular stocks in the market today, given its surging growth and cheap valuation. The stock currently has a market cap of just over $1 trillion, but I think there are two under-$1 trillion market-cap companies in the semiconductor space that are likely to surpass it in value in the next five years.

The first of these semiconductor stocks is SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY), while the second is Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

SK Hynix: The better memory play

SK Hynix and Micron compete directly in the memory market. They are two of the big three DRAM makers, along with Korean conglomerate Samsung.

Micron has arguably been outperforming SK Hynix, delivering better revenue and profit growth. However, the reason behind this is why I think SK Hynix will outperform Micron over the next five years and become the larger market cap company.

The memory market is largely being driven by demand for a specialized form of DRAM (dynamic random access memory) called high bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with graphics processing units (GPUs) and other AI chips to reduce latency and optimize performance. Demand is through the roof, with SK Hynix recently saying HBM demand was currently more than double the supply. With the big three DRAM makers dedicating much of their resources toward HBM, conventional DRAM prices have actually been rising at a quicker pace than HBM.

This dynamic has benefited Micron, which derives the least memory revenue from HBM among the group, with an HBM market share under 20%. SK Hynix, on the other hand, is the HBM leader, with about 50% market share, and it has a $500 billion long-term contract agreement with Nvidia.

Over the next five years, SK Hynix should be the company that outperforms, given that it is the technology leader in the space. Both companies currently have similar gross margins, but SK Hynix is generating more revenue and has more net cash on its balance sheet, so there is no reason it should have a lower market cap than Micron right now. As such, I expect SK Hynix's stock to outperform over the next five years.

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD: Multiple drivers

While AMD stock is not anywhere near as cheap as SK Hynix and Micron, the company has some of the best opportunities in the AI infrastructure space. The company is riding two of the biggest trends in AI: inference and agentic AI.

title: Intel Drags Down CPU Rivals. Is it a Buying Opportunity for AMD and Arm?

Intel Drags Down CPU Rivals. Is it a Buying Opportunity for AMD and Arm?

Intel's (NASDAQ:INTC) third-quarter earnings report set off a bloodbath in the semiconductor sector. The chip giant had its worst day since 1974, plunging 29% and dragging the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 7%.

Intel's third-quarter results were solid, with revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, and adjusted earnings per share more than doubled from $0.23 to $0.52, showing its turnaround efforts are paying off.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, Intel's fourth-quarter guidance sent investors fleeing, calling for a sequential decline in revenue and a 600-point decline in gross margins due to a slowdown in the PC market triggered by memory shortages. While Intel's data center and foundry businesses are growing rapidly, its client computing business, which is mostly made up of PCs, is still its biggest segment by revenue. The company forecast revenue of $15 billion-$16 billion, well below the consensus at $17.1 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of just $0.25, compared to expectations at $0.44.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why Intel's peers also fell

Intel stock has soared over the last year in part because confidence has increased in its turnaround strategy and its foundry business, but also because CPU demand is expected to soar due to agentic AI, which includes products like Meta's Muse personal AI agent.

Along with Intel, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and Arm (NASDAQ:ARM) have also significant exposure to the exposure market, and all three of those stocks are up big this year, as the chart below shows.

INTC data by YCharts

You can also see that AMD and Arm both fell sharply in sympathy with Intel, as AMD lost 11% and Arm finished down 10%.

However, the sell-off in those two stocks has as much to do with investor sentiment as it does with the implications of Intel's report.

AMD and Arm don't have as much PC exposure as Intel does, and also don't own their own foundry, meaning they aren't exposed to the capital expenditures and risk that come with it.

AMD hasn't reported third-quarter results, but in its second quarter, data center revenue made up $6.7 billion out of $11.5 billion of its revenue, while it got $3.1 billion from the client segment. Weakness in PCs will impact AMD as well, but not to the extent that it will with Intel. AMD also posted 107% growth in the data center segment in the second quarter, and there's a good chance that accelerated in the third quarter, given the massive capex spending by the hyperscalers.

detail:

The Q3 results we have already seen from 60% of S&P 500 members through Friday, October 30th, reconfirm the broad-based growth momentum we have become used to in the last few reporting cycles. While the growth pace remains strong, it does not compare favorably with other recent periods, particularly when some of the outlier results are excluded. Most importantly, the revisions trend remains positive, with estimates for 2026 Q4 and full-year 2027 continuing to rise.

We remain in the heart of the Q3 reporting season, with this week bringing in results from more than 1400 companies, including 142 S&P 500 members. This week's busy reporting line-up ranges from Tech bellwethers like Apple, Advanced Micro Devices, Palantir, and others to DuPont, McDonald's, Expedia, and many others. By the end of this week, we will have seen Q3 results from 88% of S&P 500 members.

Looking at overall expectations for the quarter, combining the actual results from the 300 S&P 500 members that have reported already with estimates for the still-to-come companies, Q3 earnings are currently expected to increase by +26.6% from the same period last year on +13.7% higher revenues, the 8th straight quarter of double-digit earnings growth for the index.

The Tech sector continues to be a major growth contributor, but the momentum is broad-based, with 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors on track to enjoy positive earnings growth and 9 generating double-digit earnings growth in Q3.

The quarterly chart below details actual results alongside Q3 2026 growth expectations and forward projections.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

As noted earlier, the revisions trend has been positive, sustaining the favorable trend in place for almost a year. Estimates for Q3 increased after the quarter got underway, and we are seeing a similar trend at play for 2026 Q4 estimates, as the chart below shows.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

This positive revisions behavior is not a new development; they extend a tailwind that has been building for nearly a year. The positive revisions were at first concentrated in Technology and, more recently, Energy, following Middle East supply disruptions. However, for 2026 Q4 and also what we saw for Q3, the favorable estimate revisions have broadened significantly, rising across 6 of the 16 Zacks sectors—including Industrials, Basic Materials, Finance, and Conglomerates alongside Tech and Energy since the start of October.

On the negative side, Q4 estimates have come down since the start of October for 10 sectors, with the major declines at the Transportation, Autos, Consumer Staples, Consumer Discretionary, Construction, and Utilities sectors.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), one of the world's largest semiconductor manufacturers, saw its shares plunge 28.58% Friday, closing at $65.76 in one of the company's steepest single-day declines in decades. The sell-off came despite Intel beating quarterly earnings expectations, as investors focused on a less encouraging outlook and growing questions about the company's turnaround.

Trading activity surged alongside the decline, with 447.8 million shares changing hands, approximately 314% above the stock's three-month average of 108.1 million shares.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,561, down 2.07%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) finished at 25,437, down 2.86%. Among semiconductor designers and foundry services for PCs, data center, and edge computing, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) closed at $504.80, down 10.88%, and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) closed at $204.64, down 4.22%, as Intel's warning pressured the group.

What this means for investors

Intel's sharp sell-off highlights growing concerns across the semiconductor industry, where investors are increasingly questioning whether strong demand for artificial intelligence can justify elevated valuations and substantial capital spending.

Despite reporting strong third-quarter revenue growth, the company issued disappointing fourth-quarter guidance, citing weakening PC demand, manufacturing constraints, and continued spending on its turnaround. These pressures raise questions about how quickly Intel can translate its investments into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

However, Intel's latest results suggest that demand for data center infrastructure remains robust. Revenue in its Data Center and AI division surged 78% year over year to $7.3 billion, supported by higher server shipments and stronger pricing. The company's immediate challenges appear more concentrated in weakening PC demand, manufacturing constraints, and substantial capital spending rather than a deterioration in its data center business.
